index: Two transaction models: ACID and BASE

sections.title: What you need first
sections.body:
- Step 4: AP systems stay available and may return stale data; designers mostly trade consistency against availability.
- Step 5: in the L4#39 quorum example there is no two-phase commit, so replicas may briefly disagree but converge eventually.

This step names that behaviour (BASE, eventual consistency) and says exactly what a reader may see while copies converge.

sections.title: Two transaction models: ACID and BASE
sections.body:
**ACID** is the relational model: strong, strict guarantees on every transaction, correctness first. Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.

**BASE** is common to NoSQL: looser guarantees that favor availability and speed at scale. Basically Available, Soft State, Eventually Consistent (L3#10).

sections.title: BASE in detail
sections.body:
From L3#11:

- **Basically Available**: a partial failure is tolerated, the rest of the system keeps serving. Replicas mean queries still succeed if a server fails.
- **Soft State**: the state is not fixed; a value may be overwritten by more recent data later on.
- **Eventually Consistent**: copies may differ briefly, then converge to the same value once replication catches up.

sections.title: Example: the address update
sections.body: A user updates her address on one server. A nearby replica updates instantly, but a data center thousands of miles away lags: briefly, the copies disagree (L3#11). Once replication catches up, they hold the same value again.

sections.title: Five strengths of eventual consistency
sections.body:
"Eventually consistent" comes in several strengths, each a different guarantee about what a reader may see (L3#12, L3#13):

- **Causal**: all copies reflect the order in which updates happened. A change to $1,000 lands everywhere before a later change to $2,000.
- **Read-your-writes**: once you write a value, your own reads always return it.
- **Session**: read-your-writes holds, but only within one session.
- **Monotonic read**: once you have seen a value, you will never see an earlier version of it.
- **Monotonic write**: your writes execute in the order you issued them, essential when operations don't commute.

sections.title: Why write order matters: Charlie
sections.body:
Charlie owes **$1,000** (L3#13).

- Apply a 10% discount, then add a $1,100 order: $900 + $1,100 = **$2,000**.
- Reverse the order: $2,100 less 10% = **$1,890**.

Same operations, different result. That is why monotonic write consistency matters when operations don't commute.

facts.text: Order first, then the discount: $2,100 less 10% = $1,890.

sections.title: Traps
sections.body:
- Trap: eventual consistency is not "no consistency". Copies converge to the same value once replication catches up (L3#11).
- Trap: session consistency is read-your-writes **limited to one session**; end the session and the guarantee may not carry over (L3#12).
- Trap: monotonic **read** is about what you see (never an earlier version); monotonic **write** is about the order your writes execute (L3#13).
- Trap: the C of ACID is transaction consistency, not CAP's replica consistency (our mapping of the two meanings in L3#4; step 4).

sections.title: Recap
sections.body:
- ACID (relational): strict guarantees, correctness first. BASE (NoSQL): availability and speed at scale.
- BASE: basically available, soft state, eventually consistent.
- Copies may differ briefly, then converge (the address example).
- Strengths: causal, read-your-writes, session, monotonic read, monotonic write.
- Charlie: the same two operations give $2,000 or $1,890 depending on order.

needs.why: BASE is the availability-first side of the CAP trade-off.
The quorum example with no two-phase commit is where replicas briefly disagree.

related.why: Next step: decide when this looser model is acceptable.

spec.intro: Match each situation to the guarantee of L3#12 and L3#13 that it describes. The situations are ours, except the last one (L3#12).

cases.scenario: You post a comment, reload the page, and always see your comment.
cases.why: Your own reads always return what you wrote.

cases.scenario: Inside one login session you always see your new profile photo; after logging in again you briefly see the old one.
cases.why: Read-your-writes, but only within one session.

cases.scenario: Once you have seen the score 2-1, you never again see 1-1.
cases.why: Reads only move forward in time.

cases.scenario: Your discount and your new order must be applied in the order you sent them.
cases.why: Your writes execute in the order you issued them; they don't commute.

cases.scenario: A balance change to $1,000 reaches every copy before a later change to $2,000.
cases.why: All copies reflect the order in which updates happened.

spec.body:
Back to the step 5 example: write to 3 replicas, wait for 2, replica 3 is written in the background.

There is **no two-phase commit**, so replicas may briefly disagree but converge eventually. That window is exactly where the five strengths matter: they say what a reader may see while replica 3 is still behind. L4#39

checkpoint.explanation: Isolation and Durability belong to ACID.

checkpoint.prompt: Charlie owes $1,000. A $1,100 order is added, then a 10% discount is applied. What does he owe?
checkpoint.explanation: $1,000 + $1,100 = $2,100, less 10% = $1,890. In the other order the result is $2,000.
checkpoint.trap: Answering $2,000, which is the discount-first order.

checkpoint.prompt: What is the difference between read-your-writes and session consistency?
checkpoint.modelAnswer: Read-your-writes means that once you write a value, your own reads always return it: you never see a value older than the one you just wrote. Session consistency gives the same guarantee but only within one session; when the session ends, the guarantee may not carry over.
